title: Training Stages & Alignment (incl. Constitutional AI)
scopeHtml: Scope: Continued pretraining vs SFT vs preference alignment, and Constitutional AI as an alternative alignment approach.

notes.title: The three training stages in one picture
notes.html:
Before any detail, here is the whole idea in plain words. A large language model (LLM, a program that predicts the next piece of text) is built in layers. Each layer uses a different kind of data and a different goal.

  1. Pretraining (and its cousin, continued pretraining): read a gigantic pile of raw text and learn to predict the next token. A token is a small chunk of text, often a word or part of a word. The goal is knowledge and language skill.
  2. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): show the model examples of the form "user asked X, ideal assistant answer was Y" and train it to imitate Y. The goal is behaviour and format.
  3. Preference alignment: show the model pairs of answers where one is better, and push it toward the better one. The goal is judgement: helpful, honest, harmless, well-toned.

Constitutional AI (Anthropic, 2022) is not a fourth stage. It is a different way to produce the preference signal in stage 3 (and some data for stage 2): instead of humans labelling which answer is better, a model labels using a short written list of principles.

 raw text (trillions of tokens)
        |
        v
 [ PRETRAINING ]  ->  base model: knows a lot, continues text, ignores instructions
        |
        v   (optional, domain data: law, medicine, your code)
 [ CONTINUED PRETRAINING ]  ->  base model that knows your domain
        |
        v   (thousands of instruction -> answer examples)
 [ SFT ]  ->  follows instructions, uses chat format
        |
        v   (pairs: chosen vs rejected answer)
 [ PREFERENCE ALIGNMENT: RLHF / DPO / RLAIF / Constitutional AI ]
        |
        v
 chat model you call over an API

Why separate stages at all? Because the data is different in size and cost. Raw text is nearly free and unlimited. Demonstrations written by experts cost real money. Comparisons ("A is better than B") are cheaper than writing answers, but still need judgement. Putting the cheap, huge stage first and the expensive, tiny stages last is the economical order.

A rough size comparison (orders of magnitude, illustrative, not exact for any named model):

 stage                 data size                 what changes
 pretraining           ~10^13 tokens (10T+)      almost all weights, all knowledge
 continued pretrain    ~10^9 to 10^11 tokens     knowledge in one domain
 SFT                   ~10^3 to 10^6 examples    behaviour, format
 preference            ~10^4 to 10^6 pairs       style, refusals, tone, honesty

See also: C1/notes/05_R1.md for the general pipeline (data cleaning, RLHF/DPO overview, RLVR). This note goes deeper on the boundaries between stages and on Constitutional AI.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "fine-tuning teaches the model new facts". SFT mostly teaches how to use what is already inside; reliable new knowledge comes from pretraining-style data or from retrieval at inference time.
  • Treating "alignment" and "RLHF" as synonyms. RLHF is one technique; DPO, RLAIF and Constitutional AI are others.
  • Forgetting that the stages are sequential: each starts from the previous stage's weights.

notes.title: Continued pretraining
notes.html:
What it is. Take an already pretrained base model and keep training it with the same next-token objective, but on a new, narrower corpus: legal contracts, clinical notes, a company's source code, a low-resource language. No instructions, no answers, just text. It is also called domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) or continual pretraining.

Why it exists. A base model has seen a little of everything but not much of your world. If your domain vocabulary is rare (drug names, internal API names, Sanskrit, a niche programming language), the model assigns low probability to the right words and makes shaky guesses. SFT with a few thousand examples cannot inject millions of facts or a new language; continued pretraining can, because it uses the same bulk-reading objective that created knowledge originally.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect domain text, clean and de-duplicate it (see the data pipeline in 05_R1).
  2. Mix in general data. A typical recipe blends the new corpus with a replay slice of general text, for example 70 percent domain and 30 percent general (illustrative; tune on your evals). Without replay the model suffers catastrophic forgetting: it gets better at the domain and worse at everything else.
  3. Use a lower learning rate than original pretraining, with a short warm-up then decay. A learning rate is the step size of weight updates; too high erases old knowledge.
  4. Train for a small number of passes over the domain data. Repeating the same documents many times leads to memorization rather than understanding.
  5. Evaluate two things: domain perplexity (does it predict domain text better?) and a general benchmark suite (did it forget?). Perplexity is how surprised the model is by text; lower is better.

Back-of-envelope cost, with the math shown. A common rule: training compute is about 6 x N x D floating-point operations, where N is parameters and D is tokens. For a 7-billion-parameter model on 2 billion domain tokens: 6 x 7e9 x 2e9 = 8.4e19 FLOPs. One H100-class GPU sustaining roughly 4e14 useful FLOPs per second (about 40 percent of a peak near 1e15, an assumption; verify for your hardware) does 8.4e19 / 4e14 = 2.1e5 seconds, about 58 GPU-hours. That is a weekend on a handful of GPUs, versus millions of GPU-hours for the original pretraining. This is why continued pretraining is attractive and why SFT alone is cheaper still.

Code. Continued pretraining is server-side GPU work, so the real snippet is Python. Kotlin and Java have no sensible training stack for this; their role is to call the resulting model through an API.

# Continued pretraining with Hugging Face transformers (plain causal LM loss).
# Prints training loss going down on domain text. Model/dataset names are placeholders.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, Trainer, TrainingArguments
from transformers import DataCollatorForLanguageModeling
from datasets import load_dataset

name = "your-org/base-model-7b"            # a BASE model, not a chat model
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name)

raw = load_dataset("text", data_files={"train": "domain_mix.txt"})["train"]
def encode(batch):
    return tok(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=2048)
ds = raw.map(encode, batched=True, remove_columns=["text"])

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="cpt-out",
    learning_rate=1e-5,                    # low: protect existing knowledge
    warmup_ratio=0.03,
    num_train_epochs=1,                    # avoid memorising the domain set
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=16,
    bf16=True,
    logging_steps=50,
)
Trainer(
    model=model, args=args, train_dataset=ds,
    data_collator=DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tok, mlm=False),  # next-token loss
).train()
// No sensible Kotlin snippet: continued pretraining needs GPU training stacks (PyTorch, DeepSpeed).
// Kotlin/Java only consume the finished model through an HTTP API, shown in later sections.
// No sensible Java snippet for the same reason (training is Python + GPU cluster work).
// Use Java to call the deployed model; see the critique-and-revision section for an SDK example.

Real products and papers. "Don't Stop Pretraining" (Gururangan et al., 2020) showed that domain-adaptive pretraining helps downstream tasks. Code Llama is Llama 2 continued on code. BloombergGPT mixed finance data with general data. Many national-language models are a Llama-style base continued on local text. Verify specifics against each paper or model card.

Production failure patterns.

  • Forgetting without replay: domain metrics improve, general reasoning and instruction following (if starting from a chat model) quietly drop. Always run a general regression suite.
  • Starting from a chat model: continued pretraining on raw text can erase the chat behaviour; if you must, redo SFT afterwards. Starting from the base model is cleaner.
  • Tokenizer mismatch: a domain full of words the tokenizer shreds into many tokens (new language, chemical names) costs context and money; sometimes you extend the vocabulary, which needs extra care for the new embeddings.
  • Data leakage: test documents hiding in the training corpus make evals look great and production look bad.

Everyday analogy. A graduate doctor (the base model) does a residency in cardiology: they keep reading and absorbing, no exam questions, just immersion in one field. They should still keep practising general medicine, or the old skills rust (replay).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing continued pretraining with SFT: the first uses raw text and the next-token loss over all tokens; the second uses instruction-answer pairs and masks the prompt.
  • Claiming it is always better than RAG. If facts change weekly, retrieval wins; weights are frozen at training time.
  • Forgetting replay data and a lower learning rate when asked how to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
  • Ignoring cost: training compute is roughly 6 x parameters x tokens, so tokens are the lever you control.

notes.title: Supervised fine-tuning, in practice
notes.html:
What it is. Show the model a conversation and train it to reproduce the assistant side. The input is a prompt (system message plus user message), the target is the ideal reply. The loss is still next-token cross-entropy, but it is computed only on the reply tokens; the prompt tokens are masked (their loss is ignored).

Why it exists. A base model, given "Write a haiku about rain", may happily continue with "Write a haiku about snow" because that looks like a list of exercises. SFT breaks that habit by showing it thousands of cases where a request is followed by an answer, then an end-of-turn token. The chat template (special tokens that mark system, user and assistant turns) is learned here.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Write guidelines: tone, length, refusals, formatting.
  2. Collect (instruction, response) pairs from experts, filtered real data, or a stronger model (checked).
  3. Render each pair with the chat template into one token sequence.
  4. Build a loss mask: 0 for prompt tokens, 1 for response tokens.
  5. Train 1 to 3 epochs at a small learning rate (about 1e-5 for full fine-tuning; higher, 1e-4 to 2e-4, is typical for LoRA, a method that trains small adapter matrices instead of all weights; verify per setup).
  6. Evaluate on held-out tasks and a safety set.

A tiny worked example of the mask:

 tokens : <user> What is 2+2 ? </user> <assistant> 4 </assistant>
 mask   :   0     0   0  0  0     0        0       1      1
 loss only on: "4" and the end token

If you forgot the mask, the model would also be trained to predict users' questions, which wastes capacity and can make it ramble in the user voice.

What SFT can and cannot do. The LIMA paper (2023) argued that about 1,000 carefully curated examples can give a strong chat model, supporting the "superficial alignment" idea: knowledge comes from pretraining, SFT mostly unlocks the format. The flip side: SFT cannot reliably teach facts the base never saw, and training on answers that contain facts the model does not know pushes it to guess confidently, which increases hallucination.

Code. The mask-by-label trick: set the label to -100 (the ignore index) for prompt tokens. Python shows real training code; Kotlin and Java show the same masking idea on plain arrays, which is useful for understanding and for data-prep tooling on a JVM backend.

# Build one SFT training example with a loss mask. Prints the labels, with -100 on the prompt.
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("your-org/base-model-7b")

prompt = "User: What is 2+2?\nAssistant: "
answer = "4" + tok.eos_token

p_ids = tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
a_ids = tok(answer, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]

input_ids = p_ids + a_ids
labels = [-100] * len(p_ids) + a_ids       # -100 = ignored by cross-entropy in PyTorch
print(labels)
// Same masking idea in plain Kotlin (data-prep tooling). Prints [-100, -100, -100, 51, 2].
fun buildLabels(promptIds: List<Int>, answerIds: List<Int>): List<Int> =
    List(promptIds.size) { -100 } + answerIds

fun main() {
    val prompt = listOf(11, 12, 13)         // pretend token ids
    val answer = listOf(51, 2)              // "4" then end-of-turn
    println(buildLabels(prompt, answer))
}
// Same masking idea in plain Java 17. Prints [-100, -100, -100, 51, 2].
import java.util.*;

public class SftMask {
    static List<Integer> buildLabels(List<Integer> prompt, List<Integer> answer) {
        List<Integer> labels = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < prompt.size(); i++) labels.add(-100);
        labels.addAll(answer);
        return labels;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(buildLabels(List.of(11, 12, 13), List.of(51, 2)));
    }
}

Real products and tools. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta all run SFT on instruction data before preference tuning. Open tooling: Hugging Face TRL SFTTrainer, Axolotl, torchtune, Unsloth. Hosted fine-tuning APIs exist at several vendors (verify which models and methods are currently offered).

Production failure patterns.

  • Template mismatch: trained with one chat template, served with another; outputs degrade mysteriously. Always use the tokenizer's own template function.
  • Style overfit: every training answer is a bulleted list, so now every answer is.
  • Missing end token: the model never learned to stop and runs to the maximum length.
  • Contaminated or low-quality data: a few hundred wrong examples can teach confident wrongness.
  • Forgetting: narrow SFT lowers general ability; mix general data or use LoRA.

Everyday analogy. An apprentice chef who already knows ingredients (pretraining) now watches the head chef plate a hundred dishes and copies the plating style and order of service. They do not learn new ingredients; they learn the restaurant's way of serving.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing that the loss is masked to the assistant tokens only.
  • Claiming SFT adds knowledge reliably; it mostly teaches format and behaviour.
  • Mixing up epochs: many epochs on small SFT data overfits and memorizes.
  • Forgetting that SFT quality and diversity matter more than count.

notes.title: Preference alignment: why a second imitation step is not enough
notes.html:
What it is. After SFT you have a model that imitates good answers. Preference alignment instead teaches it by comparison: for one prompt, here are two answers, and answer A is better than B. The model is then pushed to make A-like answers more likely and B-like answers less likely.

Why SFT alone is not enough. There are three reasons worth saying out loud in an interview.

  1. Writing a great answer is harder than judging two answers. Humans find ranking easier and more consistent than authoring. So comparisons are a cheaper, richer signal.
  2. SFT only sees positive examples. It never says "this plausible-looking answer is bad". The model has no push away from subtly harmful, sycophantic or rambling outputs.
  3. Exposure gap. SFT trains on human-written text, but at inference the model conditions on its own previous tokens. Preference training works on the model's own samples, so it corrects the mistakes the model actually makes.

Two main families.

RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback):

  1. Sample several answers per prompt from the SFT model.
  2. Humans rank them.
  3. Train a reward model (a model that outputs a single score) so that ranked-better answers score higher. The loss is the Bradley-Terry loss: -log sigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).
  4. Optimize the chat model (the policy) with RL (often PPO) to maximize the reward, minus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model. KL (Kullback-Leibler) divergence measures how far two probability distributions have drifted.

DPO (direct preference optimization): skips the reward model and the RL loop. The loss uses only log-probabilities of the chosen and rejected answers under the policy and under a frozen copy (the reference):

 margin = beta * [ (logp_pol(chosen) - logp_ref(chosen))
                 - (logp_pol(rejected) - logp_ref(rejected)) ]
 loss   = -log sigmoid(margin)

A worked number example with beta = 0.1. Suppose the policy and the reference start identical, so the margin is 0 and the loss is -log(0.5) = 0.693. After some updates the policy raises chosen log-prob by 2.0 and lowers rejected log-prob by 3.0 relative to the reference. Margin = 0.1 x (2.0 + 3.0) = 0.5. Loss = -log(sigmoid(0.5)) = -log(0.622) = 0.475. The loss fell from 0.693 to 0.475, meaning the policy moved the right way. If the policy had instead raised the rejected answer, the margin would go negative and the loss would exceed 0.693.

Code. DPO loss for one pair. Python is the real training form; Kotlin and Java compute the same scalar from four log-probabilities (useful for understanding and for offline analysis of preference logs).

# DPO loss for a single pair. Prints about 0.475 for the numbers in the text.
import math

def dpo_loss(pol_c, pol_r, ref_c, ref_r, beta=0.1):
    margin = beta * ((pol_c - ref_c) - (pol_r - ref_r))
    return -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(-margin)))

print(dpo_loss(pol_c=-8.0, pol_r=-23.0, ref_c=-10.0, ref_r=-20.0))
# policy raised chosen by 2.0 and lowered rejected by 3.0 -> margin 0.5 -> loss ~0.475
// Same DPO loss in Kotlin. Prints about 0.475.
import kotlin.math.exp
import kotlin.math.ln

fun dpoLoss(polC: Double, polR: Double, refC: Double, refR: Double, beta: Double = 0.1): Double {
    val margin = beta * ((polC - refC) - (polR - refR))
    return -ln(1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-margin)))
}

fun main() = println(dpoLoss(-8.0, -23.0, -10.0, -20.0))
// Same DPO loss in Java. Prints about 0.475.
public class Dpo {
    static double dpoLoss(double polC, double polR, double refC, double refR, double beta) {
        double margin = beta * ((polC - refC) - (polR - refR));
        return -Math.log(1.0 / (1.0 + Math.exp(-margin)));
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(dpoLoss(-8.0, -23.0, -10.0, -20.0, 0.1));
    }
}

Real products and papers. InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) popularized the SFT then reward model then PPO recipe behind ChatGPT. DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) is used widely in open models; Llama and Zephyr-style recipes use preference optimization (verify per model card). Libraries: Hugging Face TRL (DPOTrainer, PPOTrainer), OpenRLHF.

Production failure patterns.

  • Reward hacking: the policy finds quirks the reward model likes (length, confident tone, flattery). The KL penalty, reward-model ensembles and fresh human checks reduce it.
  • Sycophancy: raters often prefer agreeable answers, so the model learns to agree.
  • Over-refusal: too many "refuse when in doubt" pairs and the model declines harmless requests such as "how do I kill a child process".
  • Alignment tax: a small drop on some raw benchmarks.
  • Noisy labels: when annotators disagree 30 percent of the time, the learned signal has a low ceiling.

Everyday analogy. Instead of handing a singer a script to copy (SFT), a coach plays two takes and says "this one is better". Over many comparisons the singer develops taste, including what not to do.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying DPO has no reference model; it needs the reference log-probabilities (frozen copy or precomputed).
  • Describing the KL penalty as optional; without it the policy drifts into gibberish that fools the reward model.
  • Mixing up the reward model (a scorer) with the policy (the generator).
  • Claiming preference data can fix factual knowledge; it shifts behaviour and tone.

notes.title: Drawing the lines: which stage fixes which problem
notes.html:
Interviewers love scenario questions: "The model does X wrong; which stage do you touch?" A clean decision table gives you the answer quickly.

 Symptom                                      Likely stage to change
 -------------------------------------------  -----------------------------------------
 Doesn't know our product names / jargon      continued pretraining (or RAG if facts change)
 Continues the prompt instead of answering    SFT (chat template + instruction data)
 Wrong JSON shape, wrong answer layout        SFT (or constrained decoding, cheaper)
 Too verbose / too flattering / preachy       preference alignment (and check SFT data style)
 Refuses harmless requests                    preference data with "should answer" cases
 Answers dangerous requests                   preference / constitutional safety training
 Needs facts from last week                   retrieval or tools, not any training stage
 Weak at maths / code with checkable answers  RL with verifiable rewards (see 05_R1)

Differences by what the training signal says:

Stage Signal Loss on which tokens Typical data
Pretraining / continued "this text exists" all tokens raw documents
SFT "this is the ideal reply" reply tokens only instruction-answer pairs
RLHF / DPO "A beats B" whole sampled replies, relative ranked pairs
Constitutional AI "A beats B under these principles" same as above AI-labelled pairs

Another useful rule is the cost ladder: try prompting first, then RAG, then SFT with LoRA, then preference tuning, then continued pretraining, then training from scratch. Each rung costs roughly an order of magnitude more than the previous in data, compute and risk. Climb only when the lower rung demonstrably fails on your evals.

Code. A tiny router that picks a remedy from a symptom label. It is deliberately simple; the point is the mapping. Python first, then Kotlin and Java.

# Prints "sft" for a format problem. Plain lookup, no libraries.
REMEDY = {
    "unknown_domain_terms": "continued_pretraining_or_rag",
    "ignores_instructions": "sft",
    "bad_output_format": "sft_or_constrained_decoding",
    "too_sycophantic": "preference_alignment",
    "over_refuses": "preference_alignment",
    "stale_facts": "rag_or_tools",
}
print(REMEDY.get("ignores_instructions", "prompting_first"))
// Prints "preference_alignment".
val remedy = mapOf(
    "unknown_domain_terms" to "continued_pretraining_or_rag",
    "ignores_instructions" to "sft",
    "too_sycophantic" to "preference_alignment",
    "stale_facts" to "rag_or_tools",
)
fun main() = println(remedy["too_sycophantic"] ?: "prompting_first")
// Prints "rag_or_tools".
import java.util.Map;

public class Remedy {
    static final Map<String, String> REMEDY = Map.of(
        "unknown_domain_terms", "continued_pretraining_or_rag",
        "ignores_instructions", "sft",
        "too_sycophantic", "preference_alignment",
        "stale_facts", "rag_or_tools");
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(REMEDY.getOrDefault("stale_facts", "prompting_first"));
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Using SFT to fix a refusal problem: you add refusal-style data and make it worse. Behavioural trade-offs live in preference data.
  • Using continued pretraining to fix a fast-changing fact base: stale again in a month.
  • Skipping the baseline: teams fine-tune before measuring what plain prompting scores, then cannot show the gain.

Everyday analogy. A new hire has three gaps: they don't know the industry (immersion reading), they don't know the company's report template (training examples), they are too blunt with clients (coaching on judgement). One fix does not cover the others.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering "just fine-tune it" as the answer to every problem.
  • Choosing a training stage for facts that change often.
  • Not mentioning evals: every stage change needs a before-and-after on the same test set.

notes.title: The bottleneck Constitutional AI was built to remove
notes.html:
Human preference labelling has four weaknesses that become painful at scale:

  1. Cost and speed: tens or hundreds of thousands of comparisons, each needing careful reading.
  2. Inconsistency: different raters apply different unwritten standards; agreement is often far from perfect.
  3. Opaque values: the "values" of the model are the diffuse average of thousands of anonymous judgements. You cannot read them, audit them or edit one rule cleanly.
  4. Human exposure to harm: to train a model to refuse dangerous requests, humans must read dangerous outputs and compare them.

There is also a tension the original paper highlights: helpfulness versus harmlessness. Early RLHF models trained to be harmless often became evasive: they refused or gave vague non-answers. Raters labelling "which is less harmful" tended to reward refusal, creating over-refusal.

Constitutional AI (CAI), introduced in the 2022 Anthropic paper "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback" (Bai et al.), answers with one idea: write the standards down as a short list of natural-language principles (the constitution), and let an AI model apply them. Humans supply the principles and the helpfulness labels; the AI supplies the large volume of harmlessness judgements.

The paper's principles were drawn from sources such as the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and other published guidelines (verify exact sources in the paper). Examples of the flavour of a principle: "Choose the response that is less harmful and does not assist with illegal activity" or "Choose the response that is more honest and non-evasive". Anthropic has since published a constitution for its Claude models and discussed approaches to collecting public input on principles (verify current documents; this is fast-moving).

Real life examples. Anthropic's Claude models are trained with constitution-style methods (the company describes this publicly; the exact current training recipe is not fully public). The same RLAIF family appears in Google's work on RLAIF (Lee et al., 2023), which found AI feedback can match human feedback on some summarization and dialogue tasks.

Everyday analogy. A newsroom cannot have the editor read every article before publishing. So they write a style-and-ethics guide, train junior editors to apply it, and the editor audits samples. The guide makes the standards visible and the work scalable.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying CAI removes humans entirely. Humans write the principles and still supply helpfulness comparisons and audits.
  • Confusing "constitution" with a system prompt. The constitution is used during training to generate labels, not necessarily at inference.
  • Forgetting the motivation: scalability, transparency and avoiding evasive refusals.

notes.title: Constitutional AI phase one: critique and revision
notes.html:
CAI has two phases. Phase one is supervised: the model improves its own answers and then trains on the improved versions.

Step by step.

  1. Start with a helpful-only model (trained with human helpfulness data but not taught to refuse).
  2. Give it a red-team prompt such as a harmful or borderline request. Collect its initial, possibly harmful, response.
  3. Pick a random principle from the constitution. Ask the model: "Critique your last response according to this principle."
  4. Ask: "Rewrite the response to fix the problems found."
  5. Optionally repeat steps 3 and 4 with other principles (the paper uses multiple rounds).
  6. Collect pairs (original prompt, final revised response).
  7. SFT the model on those pairs. The result is called SL-CAI (supervised learning stage of CAI).
 red-team prompt
      |
      v
 helpful-only model --> initial answer (maybe harmful)
      |
      v   principle #k sampled at random
 "critique under principle k"  --> critique text
      |
      v
 "revise to address the critique" --> revised answer
      |
      v   (repeat with other principles)
 dataset: (prompt, final revised answer)  --> SFT --> SL-CAI model

Why the SFT stage helps: it moves the model into a region where it already refuses politely and explains, so that the later RL phase explores less and needs fewer samples. The paper also reports that critique before revision (chain-of-thought style) helps on harder cases (verify the exact finding in the paper).

Code. The loop is just three API calls. Python uses the anthropic SDK. Kotlin and Java use the official Java SDK com.anthropic:anthropic-java; the builder method names below follow its documented pattern (AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(), MessageCreateParams.builder()), but verify exact names and the response accessors in the SDK docs. Keys come from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

# Critique-and-revise one answer. Prints the revised answer text.
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()                    # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                       # verify model id in docs
PRINCIPLE = "Choose the response that is least harmful while staying honest and helpful."

def ask(text: str) -> str:
    r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=600,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}])
    return r.content[0].text

prompt = "My neighbour's wifi is locked. How do I get on it?"
draft = ask(prompt)
critique = ask(f"Prompt: {prompt}\nResponse: {draft}\n\n"
               f"Critique the response according to this principle: {PRINCIPLE}")
revised = ask(f"Prompt: {prompt}\nResponse: {draft}\nCritique: {critique}\n\n"
              "Rewrite the response so it fixes every problem in the critique.")
print(revised)       # the (prompt, revised) pair becomes one SFT training example
// Same loop in Kotlin using the Java SDK. Prints the revised answer.
// Builder and accessor names: verify in the anthropic-java docs.
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()      // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
const val PRINCIPLE = "Choose the response that is least harmful while staying honest and helpful."

fun ask(text: String): String {
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")               // verify model id
        .maxTokens(600)
        .addUserMessage(text)
        .build()
    return client.messages().create(params).content()
        .mapNotNull { it.text().orElse(null)?.text() }.joinToString("")
}

fun main() {
    val prompt = "My neighbour's wifi is locked. How do I get on it?"
    val draft = ask(prompt)
    val critique = ask("Prompt: $prompt\nResponse: $draft\n\nCritique under this principle: $PRINCIPLE")
    val revised = ask("Prompt: $prompt\nResponse: $draft\nCritique: $critique\n\nRewrite to fix the critique.")
    println(revised)
}
// Same loop in Java with anthropic-java. Prints the revised answer.
// Builder and accessor names: verify in the anthropic-java docs.
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;

public class CritiqueRevise {
    static final AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    static final String PRINCIPLE =
        "Choose the response that is least harmful while staying honest and helpful.";

    static String ask(String text) {
        MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")           // verify model id
            .maxTokens(600)
            .addUserMessage(text)
            .build();
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        client.messages().create(params).content().forEach(
            b -> b.text().ifPresent(t -> out.append(t.text())));
        return out.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String prompt = "My neighbour's wifi is locked. How do I get on it?";
        String draft = ask(prompt);
        String critique = ask("Prompt: " + prompt + "\nResponse: " + draft
            + "\n\nCritique under this principle: " + PRINCIPLE);
        String revised = ask("Prompt: " + prompt + "\nResponse: " + draft
            + "\nCritique: " + critique + "\n\nRewrite to fix the critique.");
        System.out.println(revised);
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Self-critique that agrees with itself: a model asked to critique may say "this is fine". Use principles phrased as specific tests, and sample several principles.
  • Over-sanitized revisions: revisions drift toward refusal and boilerplate, causing evasiveness. Mix in helpfulness data and measure refusal rate on benign prompts.
  • Cost: three calls per example per round; budget it (tokens x rounds x examples).
  • Data licensing: check the terms of any model used to generate training data.

Everyday analogy. A writer drafts a letter, rereads it against a checklist ("is it polite, accurate, not leaking secrets?"), rewrites it, and later the polished letters become the examples they copy from.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking phase one is reinforcement learning; it is supervised fine-tuning on self-revised outputs.
  • Forgetting that the principle is sampled at random per round, which spreads coverage.
  • Not realizing the starting point is a helpful-only model, not an already refusing one.

notes.title: Constitutional AI phase two: RLAIF
notes.html:
Phase two replaces the human harmlessness comparisons with AI comparisons. The name for the general idea is RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback.

Step by step.

  1. Take the SL-CAI model. For each red-team prompt, sample two responses.
  2. Show a feedback model the prompt, both responses, a randomly chosen principle, and ask a multiple-choice question: "Which response is better under this principle? (A) or (B)". The paper's feedback model was a pretrained model prompted this way; you can also read the probability it puts on "A" versus "B" and use it as a soft label (verify details).
  3. Result: a large dataset of AI-labelled harmlessness preference pairs.
  4. Mix with human-labelled helpfulness pairs so the model does not become uselessly cautious.
  5. Train a preference model (a reward model) on the mixed data.
  6. Run RL against the preference model (PPO in the paper), starting from SL-CAI, with the usual KL penalty. A modern alternative is to run DPO directly on the AI-labelled pairs.
 SL-CAI model --samples 2 answers--> (A, B)
                                      |
   feedback model + random principle  |   "Which is better, A or B?"
                                      v
                          AI preference label (harmlessness)
                                      |
   human helpfulness labels ----------+--> preference model (reward)
                                      |
                                      v
                          RL (PPO) or DPO  -->  final model

The paper reported that the resulting models were both more harmless and less evasive than an RLHF model trained with human harmlessness labels, a better trade-off on the helpfulness-harmlessness frontier (verify the exact plots and numbers in the paper before quoting).

A worked count to feel the economics. Suppose you want 200,000 harmlessness comparisons. A human rater doing 30 comparisons per hour needs 200,000 / 30 = 6,667 rater-hours. If an AI labeller costs on average 1,500 input tokens and 5 output tokens per comparison, total input is 200,000 x 1,500 = 3.0e8 tokens, 300 million tokens, which at an assumed 3 dollars per million input tokens (a made-up round price; verify real pricing) is 3.0e8 / 1e6 x 3 = 900 dollars. The point is the order of magnitude and speed, and also that humans can spend their time auditing a sample instead.

Code. The AI labeller as a function: given two responses and a principle, return "A" or "B". Order bias is real, so we ask both orderings.

# AI preference labelling with position-swap to cancel order bias. Prints "A" or "tie".
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"       # verify

def pick(prompt, a, b, principle):
    q = (f"Principle: {principle}\n\nUser prompt: {prompt}\n\n"
         f"(A) {a}\n\n(B) {b}\n\nWhich response better follows the principle? Answer with only A or B.")
    r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=5,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])
    return r.content[0].text.strip()[:1]

def label(prompt, x, y, principle):
    first = pick(prompt, x, y, principle)           # x shown as A
    second = pick(prompt, y, x, principle)          # y shown as A
    if first == "A" and second == "B": return "A"   # x wins both orders
    if first == "B" and second == "A": return "B"   # y wins both orders
    return "tie"                                    # inconsistent -> drop this pair
// Same position-swap labeller in Kotlin (Java SDK; verify accessor names). Returns "A", "B" or "tie".
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()

fun pick(prompt: String, a: String, b: String, principle: String): String {
    val q = "Principle: $principle\n\nUser prompt: $prompt\n\n(A) $a\n\n(B) $b\n\n" +
            "Which response better follows the principle? Answer with only A or B."
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(5).addUserMessage(q).build()
    return client.messages().create(params).content()
        .mapNotNull { it.text().orElse(null)?.text() }.joinToString("").trim().take(1)
}

fun label(prompt: String, x: String, y: String, principle: String): String {
    val first = pick(prompt, x, y, principle)
    val second = pick(prompt, y, x, principle)
    return when {
        first == "A" && second == "B" -> "A"
        first == "B" && second == "A" -> "B"
        else -> "tie"
    }
}
// Same position-swap labeller in Java (verify accessor names in the SDK docs).
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;

public class AiLabeller {
    static final AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();

    static String pick(String prompt, String a, String b, String principle) {
        String q = "Principle: " + principle + "\n\nUser prompt: " + prompt
            + "\n\n(A) " + a + "\n\n(B) " + b
            + "\n\nWhich response better follows the principle? Answer with only A or B.";
        MessageCreateParams p = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5").maxTokens(5).addUserMessage(q).build();
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        client.messages().create(p).content().forEach(
            blk -> blk.text().ifPresent(t -> sb.append(t.text())));
        String s = sb.toString().trim();
        return s.isEmpty() ? "" : s.substring(0, 1);
    }

    static String label(String prompt, String x, String y, String principle) {
        String first = pick(prompt, x, y, principle);
        String second = pick(prompt, y, x, principle);
        if (first.equals("A") && second.equals("B")) return "A";
        if (first.equals("B") && second.equals("A")) return "B";
        return "tie";
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Position and length bias in the AI judge: it prefers option A or the longer answer. Swap order, control for length, drop inconsistent pairs.
  • Inherited bias: the labeller's blind spots become the student's blind spots. Keep a human-labelled audit set and measure agreement between AI and human labels (for example Cohen's kappa).
  • Judge leakage and circularity: using the same model to generate, label and evaluate inflates scores. Evaluate with an independent judge and human spot checks.
  • Goodhart effects: the policy learns phrases the AI labeller loves ("I understand your concern, but...") and overuses them.

Everyday analogy. A school lets a trusted senior student mark the first pass of homework using the teacher's rubric, and the teacher re-marks a random sample to make sure the senior is consistent.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling RLAIF and CAI the same thing: RLAIF is the broader idea (AI feedback instead of human feedback); CAI is the specific recipe with a written constitution plus critique-and-revision.
  • Forgetting that helpfulness labels in the paper still came from humans.
  • Claiming AI feedback is always as good as human; it matches on some tasks and drifts on others, so audits remain necessary.
  • Not mentioning order bias in LLM-as-judge setups.

notes.title: Writing, testing and editing a constitution
notes.html:
The "constitution" is data, not code, but it behaves like a specification. Treat it that way.

What good principles look like.

  • Specific and testable: "Choose the response that does not give step-by-step instructions for making weapons" is easier to apply consistently than "be good".
  • Balanced: include principles that push toward helpfulness ("do not refuse reasonable requests; avoid lecturing") so safety principles do not dominate.
  • Few conflicts: when two principles collide (honesty versus kindness), the sampled one decides in that example, so conflicts become noise. Test them on borderline cases.
  • Layered: a small set of broad principles plus targeted ones for known failure areas (privacy, medical advice, minors).

How to test a principle.

  1. Build a prompt set with obvious-should-answer, borderline, and obvious-should-refuse cases.
  2. Run labelling with and without the principle; measure how often the label flips and in which direction.
  3. Compare AI labels with a small human-labelled gold set.
  4. After training, measure refusal rate on benign prompts, success rate of red-team attacks, and helpfulness scores. Change one principle at a time to attribute effects.

Editing is cheaper than relabelling. If the model turns out preachy, you add or reword a principle ("avoid moralizing"), regenerate the AI labels (hours, not weeks) and retrain. With purely human labelling you would have to re-brief and re-label.

Whose values? A constitution encodes choices. This is a governance question, not a technical one: who writes it, how it is updated, and how disagreement is handled. Anthropic has discussed experiments in gathering public input on principles (verify current status). In an interview, say the technique makes values explicit and auditable, but does not by itself make them correct.

Related techniques to know by name.

  • Constitutional Classifiers (Anthropic, 2025): separate input and output classifiers trained from constitution-style synthetic data to block jailbreaks at inference time (verify details; fast-moving).
  • Deliberative alignment (OpenAI, 2024): train a reasoning model to recall and reason over a written safety specification before answering. Same family of "teach the model written rules", applied differently (verify).
  • Model specs that vendors publish describe intended behaviour in prose and can be used for the same purpose.

Code. Store the constitution as data and sample from it, with an optional weighting to oversample principles for known weak areas.

# Sample a principle for each training example. Prints one principle string.
import random
CONSTITUTION = [
    ("harm", "Choose the response that least assists illegal or dangerous activity.", 2),
    ("honesty", "Choose the response that is more honest and non-deceptive.", 2),
    ("helpful", "Choose the response that is more helpful and avoids needless refusal.", 3),
    ("tone", "Choose the response that is less preachy or condescending.", 1),
]
weights = [w for _, _, w in CONSTITUTION]
_, text, _ = random.choices(CONSTITUTION, weights=weights, k=1)[0]
print(text)
// Weighted sampling of a principle. Prints one principle.
import kotlin.random.Random

data class Principle(val id: String, val text: String, val weight: Int)

val constitution = listOf(
    Principle("harm", "Choose the response that least assists illegal or dangerous activity.", 2),
    Principle("honesty", "Choose the response that is more honest and non-deceptive.", 2),
    Principle("helpful", "Choose the response that is more helpful and avoids needless refusal.", 3),
    Principle("tone", "Choose the response that is less preachy or condescending.", 1),
)

fun sample(): Principle {
    var r = Random.nextInt(constitution.sumOf { it.weight })
    for (p in constitution) { if (r < p.weight) return p; r -= p.weight }
    error("unreachable")
}

fun main() = println(sample().text)
// Weighted sampling of a principle. Prints one principle.
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Random;

public class Constitution {
    record Principle(String id, String text, int weight) {}
    static final List<Principle> C = List.of(
        new Principle("harm", "Choose the response that least assists illegal or dangerous activity.", 2),
        new Principle("honesty", "Choose the response that is more honest and non-deceptive.", 2),
        new Principle("helpful", "Choose the response that is more helpful and avoids needless refusal.", 3),
        new Principle("tone", "Choose the response that is less preachy or condescending.", 1));

    static Principle sample(Random rnd) {
        int r = rnd.nextInt(C.stream().mapToInt(Principle::weight).sum());
        for (Principle p : C) { if (r < p.weight()) return p; r -= p.weight(); }
        throw new IllegalStateException();
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(sample(new Random()).text());
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Vague principles: labels become noisy and the model learns nothing consistent.
  • Principle stacking: too many safety principles and too few helpfulness ones produce an evasive model; the over-refusal rate is the metric to watch.
  • Silent edits: changing the constitution without versioning makes regressions impossible to trace. Version it like code.

Everyday analogy. A company code of conduct: useful only when specific, balanced and enforced consistently; a vague one is ignored and an over-strict one paralyses staff.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying a constitution guarantees safe behaviour; it shapes training, and models can still be jailbroken or fail on novel cases.
  • Listing only harm principles; the helpfulness side is what prevents evasiveness.
  • Treating the constitution as a system prompt rather than a training-time labelling spec.

notes.title: Putting it together: a realistic end-to-end plan
notes.html:
Scenario: a bank wants an internal assistant that knows its banking policies, follows a strict answer format, refuses to give investment advice, and never leaks customer data. Walk through the stages with the cost ladder.

  1. Prompting and RAG first. A strong chat model plus retrieval over policy documents. Measure on a 200-question test set drawn from real tickets. Most of the knowledge problem is solved here, and policy updates require no training.
  2. If the format is still unreliable: SFT with LoRA. 2,000 to 5,000 reviewed (question, answer in house format) pairs. Mask the prompt. Compare against the prompting baseline. (Or use structured outputs from the API if available; it is cheaper.)
  3. If the model keeps giving investment advice or sounds too pushy: preference data. Build pairs where the chosen answer politely declines advice and points to a licensed advisor, and the rejected answer gives advice. Train with DPO. Add benign "should answer" pairs so it does not refuse ordinary product questions.
  4. To scale the safety labelling: a short constitution and AI labelling. Principles such as "do not provide personalized investment recommendations", "never reveal personal data", "answer policy questions fully and plainly". Use AI to label thousands of pairs, humans audit 5 percent.
  5. Only if the vocabulary is truly foreign (an in-house language or a huge codebase): continued pretraining on cleaned internal text with replay, then redo SFT.
  6. Gate each change with evals: capability, format, over-refusal rate, red-team success rate, and regression on a general set. Keep the previous checkpoint for rollback.
 prompt+RAG  ->  SFT (LoRA)  ->  DPO on pairs  ->  AI-labelled pairs (constitution)  -> continued pretraining
   cheapest                                                                               most expensive
   try first                                                                              try last

Latency and cost notes. Alignment stages change the weights, not the serving cost per token for a fixed model size. But a model that has been taught to be concise saves output tokens (output tokens are priced higher than input at most vendors; verify), and a model that over-refuses drives support-ticket cost. Distillation to a smaller model afterwards is a separate step with its own regression checks.

Code. A simple release gate that blocks a candidate model if it regresses on any eval. Python, Kotlin and Java versions; the same logic works in a CI job on the JVM.

# Prints "BLOCK: over_refusal" because over_refusal got worse by more than tolerance.
baseline = {"format_ok": 0.96, "over_refusal": 0.03, "redteam_success": 0.10, "general": 0.71}
candidate = {"format_ok": 0.97, "over_refusal": 0.08, "redteam_success": 0.04, "general": 0.70}
higher_is_better = {"format_ok": True, "over_refusal": False, "redteam_success": False, "general": True}
TOL = 0.02

for k, better_up in higher_is_better.items():
    delta = candidate[k] - baseline[k]
    worse = (-delta if better_up else delta) > TOL
    if worse:
        print("BLOCK:", k); break
else:
    print("PASS")
// Prints "BLOCK: over_refusal".
fun main() {
    val baseline = mapOf("format_ok" to 0.96, "over_refusal" to 0.03, "redteam_success" to 0.10, "general" to 0.71)
    val candidate = mapOf("format_ok" to 0.97, "over_refusal" to 0.08, "redteam_success" to 0.04, "general" to 0.70)
    val higherIsBetter = mapOf("format_ok" to true, "over_refusal" to false, "redteam_success" to false, "general" to true)
    val tol = 0.02
    for ((k, up) in higherIsBetter) {
        val delta = candidate.getValue(k) - baseline.getValue(k)
        if ((if (up) -delta else delta) > tol) { println("BLOCK: $k"); return }
    }
    println("PASS")
}
// Prints "BLOCK: over_refusal".
import java.util.*;

public class ReleaseGate {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Double> base = new LinkedHashMap<>(Map.of("format_ok", 0.96));
        base.put("over_refusal", 0.03); base.put("redteam_success", 0.10); base.put("general", 0.71);
        Map<String, Double> cand = Map.of("format_ok", 0.97, "over_refusal", 0.08,
                                          "redteam_success", 0.04, "general", 0.70);
        Map<String, Boolean> up = Map.of("format_ok", true, "over_refusal", false,
                                         "redteam_success", false, "general", true);
        double tol = 0.02;
        for (String k : base.keySet()) {
            double delta = cand.get(k) - base.get(k);
            double worse = up.get(k) ? -delta : delta;
            if (worse > tol) { System.out.println("BLOCK: " + k); return; }
        }
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Shipping on a single headline metric (format accuracy up) while over-refusal doubled unnoticed.
  • No rollback checkpoint when a preference run degrades tone.
  • Training and evaluation data from the same distribution, so offline metrics look better than production.
  • Treating the constitution or preference set as final; user feedback and incident reviews should feed the next round.

Everyday analogy. Renovating a house: you repaint before you rewire, and rewire before you rebuild the walls. You do the cheapest fix that cures the problem and inspect after each job.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping straight to continued pretraining or full fine-tuning without a prompting and RAG baseline.
  • Omitting over-refusal from the eval suite when training for safety.
  • Not keeping a human-audited gold set to validate AI-generated labels.
  • Describing alignment as done once shipped; it is an ongoing loop with monitoring.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Stages. Pretraining gives knowledge from raw text with next-token loss on all tokens. Continued pretraining extends that knowledge to a domain using the same loss, a lower learning rate and replayed general data to avoid forgetting. SFT teaches instruction following and format from (prompt, ideal reply) pairs with the loss masked to the reply tokens. Preference alignment (RLHF, DPO) teaches judgement from comparisons and fixes the model's own bad habits.

Constitutional AI. A short written list of principles replaces much of the human harmlessness labelling. Phase one: a helpful-only model critiques and revises its own answers under random principles, and is fine-tuned on the revisions (SL-CAI). Phase two (RLAIF): an AI feedback model compares response pairs under sampled principles, the labels are mixed with human helpfulness data, a preference model is trained, and RL (or DPO) optimizes against it. Benefits: scale, transparency, editability, less human exposure to harmful content, and less evasive behaviour. Risks: inherited labeller bias, order and length bias in the judge, vague or conflicting principles, over-refusal, and the governance question of whose values are written down.

Choosing a stage. New domain vocabulary or language: continued pretraining (or RAG if facts change). Wrong format or ignoring instructions: SFT. Wrong tone, sycophancy, refusal balance: preference data. Fresh facts: retrieval or tools. Always try prompting and RAG first and measure.

Numbers worth remembering. Training compute is roughly 6 x parameters x tokens. DPO loss starts at 0.693 when policy equals reference. A rater might do tens of comparisons per hour while an AI labeller does thousands, hence the economics of RLAIF.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Continued pretraining adds knowledge, SFT adds behaviour, preference tuning adds judgement."
  • "Constitutional AI replaces human harmlessness labels with AI labels guided by written principles, but humans still write the principles and audit."
  • "Phase one is supervised critique and revision; phase two is RL from AI feedback."
  • "Fix facts with data or retrieval, format with SFT, tone and refusals with preference data."
  • "Every stage needs a before-and-after eval, including over-refusal."

Unverified items to check before quoting. Exact principle sources and quantitative results in the CAI paper, current Anthropic constitution and Constitutional Classifiers details, Java SDK builder and accessor names, current model ids and prices, and the compute and cost figures (illustrative assumptions, with the math shown).
